newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines tightens noose for peso speculators.
newsitem.headline: Philippines tightens noose for peso speculators.

text.p: The Philippine central bank, still smarting from its surrender to currency speculators this month, on Wednesday tightened the noose for those trying again to toy with the currency.
But bankers said the measures could simply encourage the growth of two currency markets, only one of them within the central bank's control.

The central bank said it was limiting the amount of dollars onshore banks could hold and effectively barred them from selling dollars offshore in the non-deliverable forward (NDF) market, a derivatives market based in Singapore.

The two measures, which follow this month's de facto peso devaluation, will be enforced for three months to ease undue pressure on the peso, central bank governor Gabriel Singson said in a circular released on Wednesday.
While the new rulings might deter future peso speculation, currency traders said they would not flush speculators out of the system.
"This situation might trigger the rebirth of the parallel market," a senior treasury official at a foreign bank said.
Since liquidity in the official peso-dollar market will be clipped, currency hedgers will be forced to seek other channels to fund their requirements, he said.
NDFs are forward contracts where parties just pay the difference between the contracted prices without trading the underlying currency.
Banks already use subsidiaries to trade pesos and dollars outside the purview of central bank regulation.
This parallel market was sidelined during the almost two years of rock-solid stability of the peso, but has started to spring to life since the de facto devaluation nearly two weeks ago.
The central bank, which prided itself on a strong currency to control inflation, was finally beaten by speculators who had repeatedly attacked the peso.
Antonio Agcaoili, treasury head of Banco Santander Manila branch said the move might curtail speculative activity, but might also hinder demand for genuine hedging.
However, Foreign Exchange Association of the Philippines president Pedro Florescio said hedgers could still buy and sell other dollar forwards as long as the principals were delivered.

"We feel that we have to control outside forces...We always favour a free market. But if the economy is at stake, I think we have to make our priorities clear. This is just temporary," said Florescio, also first vice president of Far East Bank and Trust.
His bank was the first onshore bank allowed to trade in derivatives market. Seven other banks now have a licence.
The new tighter limit on the overbought dollar position of banks is unlikely to lead to heavy sales of the U.S. currency, a senior treasury official from a large local bank said.

"Not many banks are grossly overbought at this point," she said, adding that those which bought in the recent weeks have already sold them on the commercial clients, who were more frightened by the recent attacks on the peso.
The central bank cut the banks' overbought dollar limit to 10 percent from 20 percent of their unimpaired capital.
The banker said it would calm an edgy and tentative market.
"We are now confident that the speculators will be more careful at this point."
